newsitem.title: UK: British jobless figures boost beleaguered Major.
newsitem.headline: British jobless figures boost beleaguered Major.

text.p: A big drop in Britain's jobless total gave the ruling Conservatives a desperately needed boost on Wednesday in their campaign to get back on terms with the Labour opposition before a May 1 election.

But their political rivals questioned the reliability of the jobless figures and succeeded in steering the pre-election debate back to an area where they know the Conservatives are vulnerable -- allegations of sleaze by members of parliament.
Prime Minister John Major hailed the news that unemployment levels had fallen to their lowest levels in six years as "proof that Britain is booming."
The figures showed that 1.75 million people, or 6.2 percent of the working population -- are out of work.

But Labour leader Tony Blair, whose party is 25 points ahead of the Conservatives in opinion polls, said the figures painted a false picture because of a series of changes made by the government to the way they are calculated.
"I don't believe most people think the statistics are a true reflection of the situation," he said.

Major is banking on a string of favourable data between now and May 1 to convince Britons that his government's liberal market policies are producing an economic upturn which the rest of Europe can only regard with admiration.
He hopes that at the very least this will prevent Labour achieving the 4.3 percent swing it needs compared with the 1992 general election to win an overall majority in parliament.
But to Conservative fury, media coverage of the campaign on Wednesday focused on the delay in publishing a report into allegations of sleaze against some of its own MPs.
